title: The Mineral Detective Solving Big Problems With Rocks
summary:
Aaron Celestian is the curator of mineral sciences at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, in California. He researches minerals and how they interact with living things. "I research how we use minerals," he told TFK Kid Reporter Ian Jung. "I try to reconstruct Earth processes that happened many millions of years ago." He is also working on creating cures for diseases using minerals. "Not only am I doing all this traditional geology, but I'm also advancing the field in new pharmaceuticals," he says. "It's quite amazing."

To answer his questions, Celestian uses X-rays, lasers, nuclear reactors, radio waves and magnets. "I use everything that I can get my hands on," he says. "And if it doesn't exist yet, I build it." He is actively building his own tools and instruments to answer questions that cannot be answered without them. "I'm quite good with my hands and quite good at building things," he says, "and so I learn how to use instruments, even really complicated scientific instruments, very quickly."

One of his proudest moments came from a long experiment. His team engineered a new mineral to clean contaminated water, a project that took about 10 years of work. "We finally found a way," he says. The experiment that showed it worked, cleaning toxic lead out of water, was "extremely satisfying." He also loves walking into the museum's Gem and Mineral Hall and hearing visitors gasp in awe at the crystals on display.

Most people think his job is just looking at rocks, trimming them, making them look pretty and putting them on display, Celestian says. They do not realize he is using minerals to solve climate change problems, cure diseases, clean up the environment and tackle the energy crisis. "I think a lot of people would find mineralogy more interesting if they knew how minerals are being applied to solve some really hard problems," he says.
why_it_matters: Minerals touch everyday life in ways most people never see, from clean drinking water to new medicines, so understanding them helps solve problems that affect everyone.

background_read: Minerals are the solid, natural materials that make up rocks, and each one has its own shape, color, and makeup.
A natural history museum keeps large collections of minerals so scientists can study them and visitors can see them up close.
Scientists study minerals to learn how Earth formed and changed, and to find new ways to use them in medicine, clean water, and energy.
Some minerals can trap harmful things in water, which is why researchers test them as a way to clean up pollution.
